summary: STIR carries PASSporTs that assert caller identity in-band within SIP, or out-of-band through a storage service. This document defines how service providers can use the out-of-band approach, which helps when the call path does not preserve SIP headers.

plainLanguage.summary: Caller ID can be faked. When the proof cannot travel with the call, this lets the proof be left at a drop-off point for the receiver to pick up.

questions: passport out of band service providers
what is a call placement service
how does a cps advertisement work
how are passports retrieved from a cps
subtitle: How phone providers can leave caller-identity proofs at a drop-off service when SIP cannot carry them end to end.

tldr.problem: STIR proves who is calling by attaching a signed token (a PASSporT) to the call, but some call paths, such as legacy non-IP telephone networks, cannot carry that token in SIP headers.
tldr.mechanism: Each provider designates a Call Placement Service (CPS). Callers deposit PASSporTs there over an authenticated HTTPS connection, and the terminating provider pulls them or receives them by push. Because the CPS acts for a party to the call, the privacy machinery of the general out-of-band design is not needed.
tldr.outcome: It gives large providers a fallback when in-band STIR delivery is not universally available, at the cost of extra work to decide which providers may see which telephone numbers' PASSporTs.

facts.label: PASSporT lifetime at CPS
facts.value: At most sixty seconds (the freshness interval)

today: RFC 9888 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2026, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the out-of-band framework in RFC 8816.

sections.title: Why Out-of-Band STIR for Providers
sections.content:
The Secure Telephone Identity Revisited (STIR) framework gives cryptographic assurance of who is calling, to prevent impersonation behind robocalls, swatting, vishing and voicemail hacking. Its signed tokens are called PASSporTs. They normally travel inside SIP headers, but the STIR out-of-band framework (RFC 8816) lets them travel through a Call Placement Service (CPS) instead.

Out-of-band delivery helps when end-to-end SIP delivery is partly or fully unavailable, for example because of network border policies or because calls routinely pass through a gateway to the PSTN. The general design needs complex privacy measures so the CPS cannot learn who is calling whom. This RFC describes CPSs that act for service providers, who already know the parties to the calls, so a simpler security architecture is possible.

The RFC names carriers, large enterprises, call centers and Internet services that aggregate many telephone endpoints, including PSTN gateways and transit providers, as candidates.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally the proof of who is calling rides along with the call, like a name tag. Sometimes the call cannot carry it, so the proof is left in a mailbox the phone company runs for its own customers.

sections.title: Deployment Architecture
sections.content:
Every participating service provider is associated with one or more designated CPS instances. A caller, or sometimes a gateway, deposits a PASSporT at the CPS of the destination provider when placing a call. If the caller's domain supports in-band STIR, the deposit can happen at the same time as the in-band call. The terminating provider can run the CPS itself or have a third party run it. There is no single CPS for everyone, and several providers may share one. A CPS may also be logically distributed across distant sites that flood PASSporTs among themselves.

Reaching the CPS needs Internet connectivity, and where that exists a caller could often just start a SIP session instead. So this design applies where SIP requests cannot reliably carry PASSporTs end to end, but an HTTP transaction can reliably reach the CPS from an out-of-band authentication service (OOB-AS). The RFC hopes the need shrinks as IP connectivity between telephone providers grows, and calls it a fallback when providers cannot predict whether end-to-end SIP delivery will occur.
sections.plainLanguage: Each phone company has its own drop-off box. Callers leave their proof in the box of the company they are calling, but only when the proof cannot go along with the call itself.

sections.title: Advertising a CPS
sections.content:
When there is more than one CPS, callers need to find the right one. In small settings this can be simple provisioning, such as bilateral peering agreements or a consortium list. For wider use, the RFC defines a CPS advertisement: a JSON object that pairs telephone network resources with the URL of a CPS. It may be signed with a STIR credential or another credential the participants trust. STIR certificates carry a TNAuthList value, which can be matched against the advertisement to check the signer may advertise that CPS.

Each key is a hyphen-separated concatenation of a TNEntry type and its value: 0 for a Service Provider Code (SPC), 1 for a telephone number range, and 2 for an individual telephone number. A range is a starting number followed by a count, for example 1-15714341000-99. An advertisement can hold several pairs. CPS URIs MUST be HTTPS URIs and SHOULD be publicly reachable, though they MAY be reachable only over a closed network.

SPC-based advertising may not suit environments with no way to map a called number to an SPC, such as a national routing database, so number-based advertisements can be used instead. The RFC suggests advertisements could be held in databases, found during call routing (including by a DNS lookup), or shared among multilateral peers. An alternative is adding a field to STIR certificates that names the provider's CPS URI, which binds the URI to the provider's identifiers securely.
sections.plainLanguage: Callers need to know which drop-off box belongs to which phone company. A signed list says, for these phone numbers, use this web address.

sections.title: Submitting a PASSporT
sections.content:
In the general framework, submission is designed to keep the CPS from learning who the caller or callee is. Here the CPS belongs to the callee's provider, and the PASSporT contents are redundant with the call signaling that provider receives anyway. So this design does not try to hide the parties from the CPS.

An OOB-AS forms a secure connection to the target CPS, either per call or as a persistent connection when volumes are high. It SHOULD authenticate with mutual TLS using its STIR credential, the same one it uses to sign calls. This helps against flooding and prevents attackers from replaying captured PASSporTs to the CPS. The CPS decides for itself which OOB-AS it accepts and at what volume. Entities without a STIR credential, such as gateways and transit providers, need other mechanisms (see the gateways section).

PASSporTs need not be encrypted at rest, but TLS between the CPS and OOB-ASs is REQUIRED. An OOB-AS MUST implement a REST interface for submission as described in Section 9 of RFC 8816. If the PASSporT is also sent in-band, it can be submitted before or after the SIP request, at the originating domain's discretion. A PASSporT stays at the CPS only until retrieved, and never longer than its freshness interval, a maximum of sixty seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: The caller's phone company shows an ID badge to unlock the drop-off box, and the proof is only kept for a minute at most, so it cannot be reused later.

sections.title: Retrieving PASSporTs
sections.content:
A terminating provider's out-of-band verification service (OOB-VS) can work in one of two modes: it can pull PASSporTs after calls arrive, or it can receive pushed notifications from the CPS. CPS implementations MUST support pulling through the REST flow in Section 9 of RFC 8816.

In the pull model, the terminating provider polls the CPS after receiving a call whose signaling carries no PASSporT. Which PASSporTs an OOB-VS may receive is local policy. A CPS that serves one provider hands over everything it holds, and the CPS and OOB-VS may even be one system. In a multi-provider CPS, the terminating domain's STIR credential can determine the TNAuthList range the OOB-VS may receive, through mutual TLS or a signed token. Such a CPS must inspect the dest element of each PASSporT to route it.

In the push model, an OOB-VS can subscribe to a range of numbers or a list of SPCs. In either model the PASSporT may arrive before or after the unsigned call signaling, so the terminating side may need to delay showing a verification indicator while it waits. The exact timing, and its interaction with the substitution attack in Section 7.4 of RFC 8816, is left for future work.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiving company either checks the box when a call comes in, or asks to be told whenever something arrives for its numbers. It may need to wait a moment before saying the caller is verified.

sections.title: Gateways Between In-Band and Out-of-Band
sections.content:
A gateway may bridge in-band STIR providers and providers reachable only out-of-band. In the RFC's example, a closed network of in-band providers sends SIP INVITEs to a gateway in front of a traditional PSTN tandem serving legacy providers. The gateway extracts the PASSporT from the INVITE and stores it in a CPS set up for those legacy providers, who read it through an OOB-VS to help with robocall mitigation.

The simplest way to build this is to issue the gateway credentials allowing it to act on behalf of the legacy providers. It can then add PASSporTs to their CPS and also create PASSporTs for in-band conveyance toward terminating providers in the closed STIR network. The RFC gives a delegate certificate (RFC 9060) as an example.
sections.plainLanguage: A gateway is a translator at the border. It takes the proof from a call that carried it and drops it into the box for companies that cannot read it directly.

sections.title: Privacy and Security Considerations
sections.content:
Privacy differs from RFC 8816 because the CPS is run by a party to the call, which would see the call metadata anyway. If a third party operates the verification service for a carrier, it would see that metadata too. The RFC notes that third parties commonly receive such data for billing, security and number translation, so existing data governance agreements could apply. PASSporTs are extensible and might carry data not otherwise in SIP signaling, which those extensions would need to address. The RFC points to the origid field in RFC 8588 as an extension that might leak more information.

The Security Considerations of RFC 8816, including denial of service and traffic analysis, still apply. This design relies on STIR certificates from trust anchors the CPS already trusts, to authenticate CPS transactions and to sign advertisements. Common deployments identify providers by SPC today, and deciding whether an SPC entitles a provider to PASSporTs for a given number is not trivial but is necessary. Otherwise anyone holding a STIR certificate could obtain PASSporTs for calls in progress to any provider.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the box belongs to a company that is already part of the call, it learns nothing new. The key risk is making sure only the right company can open the right box.
